## 1. What you'll build, and why

Everything so far has been *correctness*: turn Swift into equivalent native code. Phase 4 is about
*speed* — and the whole reason we built **SIL** (concept 08) was to have a place to do it. An
optimizer isn't one big procedure; it's a **pipeline of small passes**, each a transformation
`SIL → SIL` that makes the code a little better and hands it to the next. This concept builds the
**pass manager** that runs that pipeline, plus two starter passes — so that every optimization to come
(mem2reg, constant folding, CSE, inlining) has a place to plug in.

- **You implement:** `run_pipeline` (the manager) and `constant_fold` (a pass).
- **Outcome:** `swiftml4 -O` folds and cleans up the SIL — and produces the same answers as before.

## 2. Concepts in depth

### Optimization is a pipeline

A modern optimizer is a list of **passes** run in order; each does one job and re-exposes
opportunities for the next. That's exactly swiftc's design (`SILPassManager` running a pipeline), and
ours:

![The pass manager runs a pipeline of passes (each `Sil.func -> Sil.func`), driven by `-O`. For `print(1 + 2 * 3)`: constant-fold turns the arithmetic into the literal `7`, then dead-instr-elim deletes the now-unused literals and binops.](figs/pipeline.png)

A **pass** here is `{ name; run : Sil.func -> Sil.func }` — it transforms one function. The **pass
manager** (`run_pipeline`) just folds the pipeline over each function of the module: for every
function, run pass 1, then pass 2, …. That's the entire architecture — small, composable
transformations behind a uniform interface. `--sil-opt` prints the result so you can *see* what the
passes did; `-O` runs the same pipeline right before IRGen so the native code benefits.

### The SIL your passes read and write

This concept adds no syntax — the grammar is exactly concept 13's. What it adds is a *consumer*
of the IR, so what §2 must put on the table is the **SIL** itself: your passes never see Swift
again, only this. A function is a list of basic blocks; a block is `(value, instr)` pairs in
program order ending in a terminator. Two facts decide what a pass is allowed to do with each
form — whether it is **pure** (its result is its only effect, so deleting it when nobody reads
the result is free) and whether its operands can be **substituted** (replaced by an equal value).

| printed form | `Sil.instr` | pure? | what the two passes do with it |
|---|---|---|---|
| `%3 = integer_literal $Int, 7` | `Int_lit` | yes | the folder's *source* of constants, and the value it writes back |
| `%4 = float_literal $Double, 2.5` | `Float_lit` | yes | left alone (v0 folds integers only) |
| `%5 = integer_literal $Bool, true` | `Bool_lit` | yes | left alone until concept 17 |
| `%6 = binop "+" %3, %4 $Int` | `Binop` | yes | the folder's *target*: both operands known ⇒ becomes a literal |
| `%7 = unop "-" %6 $Int` | `Unop` | yes | dead-code candidate only |
| `%8 = alloc_stack $Int  // x` | `Alloc_stack` | yes | dead-code candidate; **opaque to the folder** — this is the wall concept 16 breaks |
| `%9 = load %8 $Int` | `Load` | yes | dead-code candidate; a load is *not* a constant, whatever was stored |
| `store %3 to %8` | `Store` | **no** | never removed: the store is the visible effect |
| `%10 = function_ref @f` | `Func_ref` | yes | dead-code candidate |
| `%11 = apply %10(%3) $Int` | `Apply` | **no** | never removed: a call can print, trap or recurse |
| `%12 = apply @print(%3)` | `Print` | **no** | never removed: it *is* the observable behaviour |
| `%13 = struct (%3, %4) $P` · `struct_extract` · `struct_element_addr` | `Struct*` | yes | dead-code candidates |
| `%14 = enum #1(%3) $E` · `enum_tag` · `enum_payload` | `Enum*` | yes | dead-code candidates |
| `br bb2` · `cond_br %5, bb1, bb2` · `return %3` · `trap "…"` | `term` | — | untouched in this concept; concept 17 folds `cond_br` |

The "pure?" column *is* `dead_instr_elim`'s rule, and it is given to you for exactly that reason:
the interesting half of a DCE is the list of things it must not touch. Concept 16 adds block
**arguments** to the terminators and concept 17 starts rewriting them; until then a pass edits
`block.instrs` and nothing else.

### Two starter passes, and why order matters

- **Constant folding** walks the instructions, tracking which SIL values are known integer constants,
  and replaces a `binop` of two constants with the literal result — so `1`, `2`, `3`, `*`, `+` collapse
  the `1 + 2 * 3` into `integer_literal 7`. `÷0` and `%0` are never folded: there is no value to
  replace them with — Swift traps there. (Honesty note: swiftc prints `Fatal error: Division by
  zero` and exits 133; our IRGen still emits a bare `sdiv`/`srem`, so *our* binary's behaviour on
  `x / 0` is undefined rather than a trap. That is an open gap in the code generator, PROOFREAD.md
  §6, not something a fold can fix — the oracle corpus keeps `÷0` out for that reason.)
- **Dead-instruction elimination** then removes any *pure* instruction whose result nobody uses. After
  folding, the original literals and binops are dead, so DCE deletes them.

Run them in the other order and you'd accomplish nothing — there's no dead code until folding creates
it. That's the first lesson of a pass pipeline: **passes enable each other**, and ordering is part of
the design (swiftc tunes its pipeline carefully, and re-runs cleanup passes after big transforms).

### The non-negotiable invariant: behavior is preserved

An optimization that changes what the program *prints* is a bug, not an optimization. Every pass must
preserve observable behavior, which is why `-O` output must match `-Onone` (and `swiftc`) exactly —
the optimizer is held to the same parity bar as the compiler. (It's also why DCE keeps anything
side-effecting — a `store`, an `apply`, a `print` — no matter whether its *result* is used.) The SIL
**verifier** runs twice — on the SIL SILGen produced, and again on what the pipeline returned, so
a pass that branched to a block it deleted or left a block without a terminator is caught in the
driver rather than in IRGen or, worse, at run time.

Parity is only a fair test if the corpus stays inside what both compilers mean the same, and the
front end is what enforces that. Three refusals draw that line, and `sema-subset.t` records them:

| program | our message | swiftc |
|---|---|---|
| `print(p)` for a struct, `print(e)` for an enum, `print(o)` for an optional | `cannot print a value of type 'P' (only Int, Double, Bool and String)` | **accepts** — prints `P(x: 1)`, `a`, `Optional(5)`. Our `print` lowers one scalar to `printf`, so we refuse rather than emit ill-typed IR |
| `a == b` on two structs | `binary operator '==' cannot be applied to two 'P' operands` | same wording (`diag::cannot_apply_binop_to_same_args`) |
| `a == b` on two optionals | `binary operator '==' cannot be applied to two 'Int?' operands` | **accepts** — `Int?` is `Equatable`. We support only `o == nil`, which reads the tag |
| `c.k = 5` on a `let` property | `cannot assign to property: 'k' is a 'let' constant` | same wording (`diag::assignment_lhs_is_immutable_property`) |

Two of those are divergences, not agreements — swiftc accepts what we refuse. That is the honest
position: refusing early is how a subset stays testable, and the alternative (letting the program
through to IRGen) is a miscompile, which is worse than a diagnostic.

### Why these passes are weak *right now* — and the setup for mem2reg

Try folding `let x = 1; let y = 2; print(x + y)`. It won't fold to `3` — because `x` and `y` live in
**`alloc_stack` slots**, so `x + y` is really `add (load x_slot) (load y_slot)`, and our
constant-folder only sees literal *values*, not values that *came from a load of a slot that was
stored a constant*. The memory indirection blocks the analysis. **This is the whole motivation for
concept 16.** `mem2reg` promotes those stack slots to SSA values — turning `load x_slot` into the
constant `1` directly — and suddenly constant folding, CSE, and everything else can *see through* what
used to be loads and stores. The raw, memory-based SIL we've emitted since concept 08 was the
deliberate setup; mem2reg is the unlock, and these passes are why it matters.

> Oracle: `swift/lib/SILOptimizer/PassManager/PassManager.cpp` runs the pipeline;
> `Transforms/`/`Mandatory/` are the passes. swiftc separates *mandatory* passes (always run, for
> correctness — like definite-init) from *performance* passes (only at `-O`). Ours is one perf
> pipeline; the split is an exercise.

## 4. Test it

```bash
make lab C=phase4-optimizer/15-pass-manager
```

Two cram files, one per hole, plus the subset file, a unit suite and the oracle — in the order
you fill the holes:

- `opt-pipeline.t` — `--sil-opt` with the pipeline's *given* pass only: `let a = 1; a + 1;
  print(a)` has a dead binop (it reads `a` from a slot, so folding could never touch it) that
  `dead_instr_elim` removes — once `run_pipeline` actually runs it. Also: the `store` and `print`
  survive, a dead binop inside a *second* function goes too, both functions are still there, and
  `-O` builds a binary that prints the same thing. Green with `run_pipeline` alone.
- `opt-fold.t` — `--sil-opt` on literal arithmetic: `1 + 2 * 3` → `integer_literal 7` with no
  binop left; a chain to `10`; truncating `/` and `%` on negatives; `10 / 0` and `10 % 0` left
  as binops beside a `10 / 2` that folds; a comparison left alone; a binop of two loads left
  alone beside a literal one that folds; and two `-O` runs (`7`, `10`; a loop that still prints
  `20`). Every count is printed raw, then optimized, so the diff says what changed.
- `sema-subset.t` — GIVEN code, so it is `PASS` before you write a line: the four refusals that
  keep an aggregate out of IRGen (printing a struct, enum or optional; `==` on a struct or an
  optional; assigning a `let` property; assigning any property of a `let` binding), each beside
  the program it accepts. It is in the roster because the oracle below is only a fair test while
  the corpus stays inside the subset, and this file is where that boundary is written down.
- `test_opt.ml` (alcotest `opt`) — the same in-process: the manager runs the given pass, is the
  identity on an empty pipeline, visits every function with the passes in order, and feeds each
  pass's result to the next (a spy pass records what it saw); `constant_fold` called directly on
  `main` for each rule above; then `Opt.optimize` end to end. Counts are taken *before* optimizing
  — passes mutate blocks in place, so a "before" measured afterwards is already the "after".
- `oracle.t` — **the headline**: every program in `oracle-corpus.txt` (18: loops with side
  effects, recursion, nested `break`/`continue`, structs, enums + `switch`, optionals, a
  force-unwrap of `nil`, an optional stored property, a `let` property, a `Double` field, and a
  few foldable ones) is built four ways — `swiftc -Onone`,
  `swiftc -O`, `lab build`, `lab build -O` — and all four binaries must print the same stdout
  and exit with the same code. This is the optimizer's invariant made mechanical: a pass that
  changes an answer fails here, whatever the shape checks say.

A hole you have not started shows as `TODO` with the list of what it will check; a hole in
progress shows `FAIL` with, under each failing case, what the test wants and what your code
printed. The oracle passes on the untouched skeleton — an identity pipeline preserves behaviour
trivially — and keeps passing as long as your passes do.

## 5. Benchmark it

Compare `-O` vs `-Onone` on a constant-heavy program — you'll see a small win (less arithmetic at
runtime). The *big* wins are still ahead: after mem2reg (16) these passes reach through memory, and
inlining (19) + LLVM's backend (20) close most of the gap to `swiftc -O`. Tracking the metric pass by
pass is the point of Phase 4.

## 6. Exercises

1. **A peephole pass.** `x + 0 → x`, `x * 1 → x`, `x * 0 → 0`, `x - x → 0`. Algebraic identities that
   don't need both operands constant — a different shape of pass from folding.
2. **An analysis (not a transform).** Write `instruction_count : Sil.func -> int` and a pass that just
   *logs* per-function stats. Analyses inform transforms; this is the seed of a cost model (concept 19).
3. **Dead-block elimination.** Remove blocks unreachable from the entry (a graph reachability over the
   terminators) — and watch it clean up the `unreachable` blocks SILGen leaves after returning switches.
4. **Mandatory vs. performance passes + a fixed point.** Split the pipeline into always-run and
   `-O`-only, and run the `-O` pipeline to a **fixed point** (repeat until a pass makes no change), so
   fold→DCE→fold cascades fully.

## 7. Recap & what's next

You built the optimizer's spine: a **pass** is a `SIL → SIL` transform, the **pass manager** runs a
pipeline, `-O` applies it, `--sil-opt` shows it — and it all **preserves behavior**. Two starter
passes (constant folding, DCE) proved the pipeline works and showed how passes enable one another.

Next is the one you've been waiting for since concept 08: **16-mem2reg-ssa**. The raw,
`alloc_stack`/`load`/`store`-heavy SIL gets promoted to **SSA** — values defined once, threaded through
**basic-block arguments** (swiftc's "phi"). It's a from-zero SSA lesson — **dominator trees**,
where to place the block arguments, and a **renaming** walk — and it's what turns the weak passes here
into powerful ones, because they finally see *through* memory.

## 8. Appendix — full solution

From `solution/opt.ml`:

```ocaml
let run_pipeline ?(log = false) (passes : pass list) (m : Sil.modul) : Sil.modul =
  let run_func (f : Sil.func) =
    List.fold_left
      (fun f p ->
        if log then Printf.eprintf "  sil-opt: [%-16s] @%s\n" p.name f.Sil.fname;
        p.run f)
      f passes
  in
  { m with Sil.funcs = List.map run_func m.Sil.funcs }

let constant_fold (f : Sil.func) : Sil.func =
  let lit : (Sil.value, int) Hashtbl.t = Hashtbl.create 64 in
  let fold (v, instr) =
    (match instr with Sil.Int_lit n -> Hashtbl.replace lit v n | _ -> ());
    match instr with
    | Sil.Binop (op, a, b) -> (
        match (Hashtbl.find_opt lit a, Hashtbl.find_opt lit b) with
        | Some x, Some y -> (
            match eval_binop op x y with
            | Some n -> Hashtbl.replace lit v n; (v, Sil.Int_lit n)
            | None -> (v, instr))
        | _ -> (v, instr))
    | _ -> (v, instr)
  in
  List.iter
    (fun (b : Sil.block) -> b.Sil.instrs <- List.rev_map fold (List.rev b.Sil.instrs))
    (List.rev f.Sil.blocks);
  f
```

## 9. Exercise solutions

### 1 — peephole

A second pass like `constant_fold`, but matching algebraic identities: a `Binop (Add, a, b)` where `b`
is the literal `0` becomes a copy of `a` — i.e. replace later uses of the result with `a` (a tiny
*copy propagation*), or, more simply, rewrite the instruction's result to alias `a` and let DCE remove
it. `x * 0` becomes `integer_literal 0`. These don't need *both* operands constant, so they catch cases
folding misses.

### 2 — an analysis

`instruction_count f = List.fold_left (fun n b -> n + List.length b.Sil.instrs) 0 f.Sil.blocks`. Wrap
it in a pass whose `run` logs the count and returns `f` unchanged. Analyses are passes that *compute*
rather than *transform*; the inliner (concept 19) is a transform driven by exactly this kind of
cost analysis.

### 3 — dead-block elimination

BFS/DFS from the entry block (`bid = 0`) following `Br`/`Cond_br` targets; any block not reached is
dead. Filter `f.Sil.blocks` to the reachable set. This removes the trailing `unreachable` blocks
SILGen emits after an exhaustive returning `switch`, shrinking the IR with no behavior change.

### 4 — mandatory/performance + fixed point

Tag each pass `Mandatory | Performance`; `-Onone` runs only the mandatory ones, `-O` runs both. For the
fixed point, make passes return whether they changed anything (`Sil.func -> Sil.func * bool`) and loop
the `-O` pipeline until a full sweep reports no change — so `fold → DCE → fold` cascades converge
instead of stopping after one round.
```
